title: Black-body radiation; Stellar luminosity, brightness and distance; Doppler effect; Expanding universe and cosmology
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: A01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; A01-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; T04-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; T04-1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: A01-1#N.7a, A03-1#N.6, A03-2#N.3, A03-3#N.3, T04-1#N.3, W11-1#N.6, A01-1#N.12b, A03-1#N.8, A03-2#N.5, A03-3#N.6, T04-1#N.8, W11-1#N.13a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Luminosity
items.clue: Total power a star emits, measured in watts.

items.label: Black body
items.clue: Type of emitter that a star closely resembles.

items.label: Peak wavelength
items.clue: Position of the top of the spectrum curve: about 500 nm for the Sun, 850 nm for a red star.

items.label: Stefan–Boltzmann law
items.clue: States that total power radiated is proportional to surface area times T to the fourth power.

questions.stem: Two measurements of the position of a nearby star against very distant background stars, made six months apart, differ by an angle of 0.0700 arc-second. Take 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, 1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m and 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m. What is the distance to the star in AU?
Andromeda, our nearest large neighbour galaxy, shows a blue shift. Does this contradict the expansion of the universe?

options.text: Yes: in an expanding universe, every galaxy must be moving away from us.
No: space is contracting in our part of the universe, drawing Andromeda in.
No: its light looks blue because Andromeda contains many hot, blue stars.
No: at so short a distance, its own motion towards us outweighs expansion.

questions.explanation: Cosmological red shift is tiny over so short a journey. Andromeda's motion through space towards us gives a larger Doppler blue shift.

questions.stem: A galaxy at a distance of 1.2 × 10²⁴ m recedes from the Earth at 2800 km s⁻¹. What value of the Hubble constant does this give?
questions.explanation: H₀ = speed ÷ distance = 2.8 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ ÷ 1.2 × 10²⁴ m = 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹.

questions.stem: As the universe expands, which of these distances increases?

options.text: The diameter of our own galaxy, the Milky Way
The distance from the Earth to the Sun
The distance between two far-apart galaxy clusters
The diameter of a hydrogen atom in a gas cloud

questions.explanation: Distant clusters are not bound to each other, so the expansion of space between them carries them apart.

questions.stem: Predict first. A black body is heated to a higher temperature. How does its emission spectrum change?

options.text: It emits more at every wavelength, and the peak moves to a longer wavelength.
It emits more at every wavelength, and its peak moves to a shorter wavelength.
Its peak moves to shorter wavelengths, so it emits less at long wavelengths.
It emits only one wavelength, λ_max, which gets shorter as it gets hotter.

questions.stem: A spectral line of hydrogen has a wavelength of 656.3 nm when measured in the laboratory. A galaxy is moving directly away from Earth at 3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. At what wavelength is this line observed in the spectrum of the galaxy?
Stars X and Y have the same surface temperature. X has twice the radius of Y. The parallax angle of X is half that of Y. Which statement is correct?

options.text: X is 4 times as luminous as Y and twice as far away.
X is 4 times as luminous as Y and half as far away.
X is twice as luminous as Y and twice as far away.
X and Y are equally luminous, because they have the same temperature.

questions.explanation: L ∝ r²T⁴: same T, double r → 4 × L. d = 1/p: half the parallax → twice the distance.

questions.stem: A hydrogen absorption line has a laboratory wavelength of 656.28 nm. In the spectrum of a star in our own galaxy, it is observed at 656.08 nm. What is the star's velocity along the line of sight?

options.text: 9.1 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ away from the Earth

questions.stem: A value of the Hubble constant is 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Take 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m. What is this in km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹?
questions.explanation: 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 3.09 × 10²² = 7.4 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ per Mpc = 74 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.

questions.stem: The cosmic microwave background peaks at about 1.1 mm today. Since it was released, its wavelengths have been stretched by a factor of about 1100. At about what wavelength did it peak when it was released?
questions.explanation: 1.1 × 10⁻³ m ÷ 1100 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. By Wien's law that is a black body at about 2900 K: the glow of the hot early universe.

questions.stem: A small metal sphere of radius 5.0 cm is heated to 527 °C. Treat it as a black body and take σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What power does the sphere emit as thermal radiation?

A calcium absorption line has a wavelength of 393.4 nm in the laboratory. In the spectrum of a distant galaxy the same line is at 401.3 nm. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the galaxy's velocity relative to Earth?
questions.explanation: Δλ = 7.9 nm; v = c × 7.9/393.4 = 6.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Longer wavelength → receding.
